questions.set_title: Banks, credit unions, and what they do
questions.section_skill: Explain what banks and credit unions do with deposits and loans
questions.intro: A bank is a business that accepts deposits (money people put in accounts) and makes loans (money it lends and expects to be paid back with interest). Banks keep only part of their deposits as cash and lend much of the rest. The interest borrowers pay helps the bank pay its costs, earn a profit, and pay interest to savers.
questions.question: Maya deposits $500 of her summer earnings at a bank. What does the bank usually do with much of the money while it sits in her account?

choices.text: Lends part of it to other customers, such as car buyers or businesses
Keeps her exact bills in a locked box with her name on it
Sends it to the government until she withdraws it
Invests all of it in the stock market on Maya's behalf, and she keeps any gains

questions.correct_answer: Lends part of it to other customers, such as car buyers or businesses

misconceptions.B: Thinks a bank stores each customer's own cash separately
misconceptions.C: Confuses a bank deposit with a tax payment
misconceptions.D: Confuses a bank deposit with an investment account

questions.feedback: Banks pool deposits and lend much of the money to borrowers. Maya can still withdraw her $500; the bank keeps enough cash and reserves on hand to meet withdrawals.

questions.set_title: Banks, credit unions, and what they do
questions.section_skill: Explain what banks and credit unions do with deposits and loans
questions.intro: A credit union offers many of the same services as a bank: checking and savings accounts, debit cards, and loans. The difference is ownership. A credit union is a not-for-profit cooperative owned by its members, who are its account holders. To join, you must meet its membership rules, such as living in an area, working for an employer, or belonging to a group.
questions.question: Which statement best describes a credit union?

choices.text: A not-for-profit financial cooperative owned by its members
A government office that issues credit cards
A company that only sells stocks and bonds
A bank owned by outside investors who buy its stock and are not its customers

questions.correct_answer: A not-for-profit financial cooperative owned by its members

misconceptions.B: Thinks "credit" in the name means the government provides credit
misconceptions.C: Confuses a credit union with a brokerage firm
misconceptions.D: Describes a stock-owned bank, not a credit union

questions.feedback: Credit unions are member-owned, not-for-profit cooperatives. Profits are returned to members through lower fees, lower loan rates, or higher savings rates.

questions.set_title: Banks, credit unions, and what they do
questions.section_skill: Explain what banks and credit unions do with deposits and loans
questions.intro: Every credit union has a "field of membership": the group of people it is allowed to serve. It might be employees of certain companies, people who live or work in a county, or members of an organization. Family members of current members can often join too. Some credit unions let almost anyone join by first joining a partner organization.
questions.question: Jordan wants to join Riverside Teachers Credit Union, but Jordan is not a teacher and has no family member who works in a school. What is the most likely obstacle?

choices.text: Credit unions do not offer checking accounts
Jordan must buy stock in the credit union on a stock exchange
Credit unions only accept customers who already have a credit card
Jordan may not meet the credit union's membership rules

questions.correct_answer: Jordan may not meet the credit union's membership rules

misconceptions.A: Thinks credit unions offer only loans
misconceptions.B: Confuses member ownership with buying publicly traded shares
misconceptions.C: Thinks a credit card is required to open an account

questions.feedback: A credit union can serve only people within its field of membership. Jordan should check its eligibility rules or look for a credit union whose field includes Jordan.

questions.set_title: Banks, credit unions, and what they do
questions.section_skill: Explain what banks and credit unions do with deposits and loans
questions.intro: Banks come in different types. National and regional banks are large and have many branches. Community banks are smaller and local. Online banks have no branches; customers use an app, a website, ATMs, and mobile deposit. Deposits at federally insured banks are protected by the FDIC, and deposits at federally insured credit unions by the NCUA, up to legal limits.
questions.question: A city has a large national bank, a local community bank, a credit union, and an online-only bank. Which feature is TRUE of all four kinds of institutions?

choices.text: They can offer federally insured deposit accounts
They are all owned by the customers who keep accounts there
They all have branches where you can deposit cash in person
They all guarantee a profit on money you invest with them

questions.correct_answer: They can offer federally insured deposit accounts

misconceptions.B: Credit union ownership applied to every institution
misconceptions.D: Confuses insured deposits with guaranteed investment returns

questions.feedback: Federally insured banks (FDIC) and credit unions (NCUA) can all offer insured deposit accounts. Ownership, branches, and fees differ from one institution to another.

questions.set_title: Banks, credit unions, and what they do
questions.section_skill: Explain what banks and credit unions do with deposits and loans
questions.question: Priya keeps $1,200 in cash in a shoebox. Which risk would a federally insured bank account reduce?

choices.text: The money buying less in the future because prices rise
Having to pay sales tax when she spends the money
Spending the money on things she does not need
Losing the money to a fire or theft at home

questions.correct_answer: Losing the money to a fire or theft at home

misconceptions.A: Thinks a bank account removes the effect of inflation
misconceptions.B: Confuses where money is kept with taxes on purchases
misconceptions.C: Thinks an account controls spending habits by itself

questions.feedback: Insured deposits are protected from loss at home and from bank failure up to legal limits. An account does not stop prices from rising and does not decide how she spends.

questions.set_title: Banks, credit unions, and what they do
questions.section_skill: Deposits, withdrawals, and loans
questions.intro: A deposit is money you put into an account. A withdrawal is money you take out. A loan is money a lender gives you that you must pay back, usually with interest.
questions.question: Aiden puts $40 into his savings account. What is this called?

choices.text: A withdrawal
A loan
A fee
A deposit

questions.correct_answer: A deposit

misconceptions.B: Thinks putting money in is borrowing
misconceptions.C: Confuses adding money with a charge

questions.feedback: Putting money into an account is a deposit. Taking money out is a withdrawal.

questions.set_title: Banks, credit unions, and what they do
questions.section_skill: Deposits, withdrawals, and loans
questions.intro: When you take money out of your own account, by cash at an ATM, a debit card purchase, or a check, it is a withdrawal. The money was already yours.
questions.question: Sofia takes $60 in cash out of her checking account at an ATM. What is this called?

choices.text: A withdrawal
A deposit
A loan from the ATM company
Interest

questions.correct_answer: A withdrawal

misconceptions.D: Confuses money taken out with money earned

questions.feedback: Taking your own money out of your account is a withdrawal; you do not owe it back.

questions.set_title: Banks, credit unions, and what they do
questions.section_skill: Deposits, withdrawals, and loans
questions.intro: A loan is borrowed money. The borrower promises to repay the amount borrowed, called the principal, plus interest, which is the price of borrowing.
questions.question: A bank gives Luis $8,000 to buy a used car, and Luis agrees to pay it back over four years with interest. What did Luis receive?

choices.text: A loan
A deposit
A gift from the bank
A withdrawal from his savings

questions.correct_answer: A loan

misconceptions.B: Thinks money received from a bank is a deposit
misconceptions.D: Confuses borrowed money with his own savings

questions.feedback: Money that must be repaid with interest is a loan. Luis owes the $8,000 principal plus interest.

questions.set_title: Banks, credit unions, and what they do
questions.section_skill: Deposits, withdrawals, and loans
questions.intro: Interest works in two directions. A borrower pays interest to a lender for using the lender's money. A saver earns interest from a bank, because the bank uses the saver's deposits to make loans.
questions.question: Which choice describes interest from a SAVER'S point of view?

choices.text: Money you pay the bank each month to keep your savings account open
The amount you first deposited
A tax on savings accounts
Money the bank pays you for keeping your money in an account

questions.correct_answer: Money the bank pays you for keeping your money in an account

misconceptions.A: Confuses interest with a monthly fee

questions.feedback: Savers earn interest; borrowers pay interest. The first amount deposited is the principal.

questions.set_title: Banks, credit unions, and what they do
questions.section_skill: Deposits, withdrawals, and loans
questions.question: Why can a bank afford to pay interest to savers?

choices.text: It charges borrowers a higher interest rate than it pays savers
The federal government pays the interest on every insured savings account
It charges savers a fee equal to the interest
It prints new money to pay interest

questions.correct_answer: It charges borrowers a higher interest rate than it pays savers

misconceptions.C: Thinks interest is cancelled by a fee
misconceptions.D: Confuses a bank with the central bank

questions.feedback: A bank earns more interest from loans than it pays on deposits. The difference helps cover costs and profit.

questions.set_title: Banks, credit unions, and what they do
questions.section_skill: Online banks, apps, and partner banks
questions.intro: Many apps that hold money are not banks. They are financial technology ("fintech") companies that partner with a bank. Money may be FDIC insured only if it is actually deposited at the partner bank in the customer's name and the records are kept properly. If the fintech company itself fails, getting access to money can take time.
questions.question: A payment app advertises "bank-level" accounts. Its fine print says, "We are a financial technology company, not a bank. Banking services are provided by Harbor Bank, Member FDIC." What does this mean?

choices.text: The app company is itself an FDIC-insured bank, so it is fully protected
No money in the app can ever be insured
Harbor Bank guarantees the app company's profits
Harbor Bank holds the deposits; the app company itself is not a bank

questions.correct_answer: Harbor Bank holds the deposits; the app company itself is not a bank

misconceptions.A: Takes the advertising at face value
misconceptions.B: Ignores insurance through a partner bank
misconceptions.C: Misreads what a partner bank does

questions.feedback: The fine print says the deposits are at Harbor Bank. FDIC insurance protects against Harbor Bank failing, not against the app company failing.

questions.set_title: Banks, credit unions, and what they do
questions.section_skill: Online banks, apps, and partner banks
questions.intro: Deposit insurance covers money in deposit accounts at insured banks. A balance kept in a payment app may not be a bank deposit at all, depending on how the app holds it. The app's terms explain where the money is held.
questions.question: Which question is MOST useful to ask before keeping a large balance in a payment app?

choices.text: How many millions of people already use and trust the app?
Does the app have a nice design?
Can I send money to friends instantly?
Is my balance held at an FDIC-insured bank in my name?

questions.correct_answer: Is my balance held at an FDIC-insured bank in my name?

misconceptions.C: Focuses on features rather than protection

questions.feedback: Whether the balance is a deposit at an insured bank, in your name, decides whether deposit insurance can apply.

questions.set_title: Banks, credit unions, and what they do
questions.section_skill: Online banks, apps, and partner banks
questions.intro: Online banks often pay higher savings rates and charge fewer fees because they have no branches to run. The trade-off is access: depositing cash can be hard or impossible, and help is by phone or chat. The best choice depends on how you use your money.
questions.question: An online bank pays 4.0% on savings and charges no monthly fee, but it has no branches. A local bank pays 0.5% and has a branch near Ana's job. Ana is paid in cash tips each night. Which drawback of the online bank matters MOST for Ana?

choices.text: Depositing cash may be difficult without a branch
The online bank's savings rate is too high
Online banks are not allowed to give customers debit cards
Online banks are never insured

questions.correct_answer: Depositing cash may be difficult without a branch

misconceptions.B: Thinks a higher savings rate is a drawback
misconceptions.C: Assumes online banks lack debit cards
misconceptions.D: Assumes no online bank is insured

questions.feedback: Ana deposits cash every night, so a way to deposit cash matters more to her than a higher rate. She might use both kinds of bank.

questions.set_title: Banks, credit unions, and what they do
questions.section_skill: Online banks, apps, and partner banks
questions.question: A bank's website shows the FDIC logo. What does this tell a customer?

choices.text: The bank's stock price is guaranteed
Its deposits are insured up to the legal limit
Every product the bank sells is insured, including investments
The bank charges no fees

questions.correct_answer: Its deposits are insured up to the legal limit

misconceptions.A: Thinks FDIC insures a bank's stock

questions.feedback: The FDIC sign means deposits are insured up to $250,000 per depositor, per insured bank, per ownership category. Investments sold at a bank are not deposits and are not FDIC insured.

questions.set_title: Banks, credit unions, and what they do
questions.section_skill: Online banks, apps, and partner banks
questions.question: Which situation shows the main risk of keeping money with a non-bank app?

choices.text: The partner bank pays interest into each customer's account every month
The app sends a monthly statement
The customer uses the app's debit card at a store
The app company fails and customers wait months to reach their money

questions.correct_answer: The app company fails and customers wait months to reach their money

misconceptions.A: Describes an advantage, not a risk

questions.feedback: When a fintech company fails, its records of who owns what must be sorted out before customers can get their money, even if a partner bank is insured.

questions.set_title: Banks, credit unions, and what they do
questions.section_skill: Comparing financial institutions
questions.intro: Fees add up. A monthly fee costs 12 times that amount in a year. Many banks waive a monthly fee if you meet a condition, such as a minimum balance or a direct deposit. If you will not meet the condition, plan to pay the fee.
questions.question: Two banks are similar except: Bank A charges a $12 monthly fee unless the balance stays above $1,500; Bank B charges no monthly fee. Kai usually keeps about $400 in checking. How much more would Bank A cost Kai per year?

misconceptions.B: Uses one month instead of a year

questions.feedback: Kai's $400 balance is below $1,500, so the fee applies every month: $12 × 12 = $144.

questions.set_title: Banks, credit unions, and what they do
questions.section_skill: Comparing financial institutions
questions.intro: When comparing institutions, start with how you will use the account: fees, ATM access, branch or app access, minimum balances, and the savings rate. A feature that matters to one person may not matter to another.
questions.question: Which comparison is MOST important for a student who will make frequent ATM withdrawals?

choices.text: How many fee-free ATMs are near home and school
Whether the bank sponsors a local sports team or event
The color of the debit card
The bank's auto loan rate

questions.correct_answer: How many fee-free ATMs are near home and school

misconceptions.D: Compares a product the student will not use now

questions.feedback: Frequent ATM users can pay fees each time they use an out-of-network ATM, so fee-free ATM access is the key comparison.

questions.set_title: Banks, credit unions, and what they do
questions.section_skill: Comparing financial institutions
questions.intro: To compare savings rates, find the interest each account pays. For one year, interest ≈ balance × rate (with the rate written as a decimal). Then subtract.
questions.question: A credit union and a bank both offer free checking. The credit union pays 2.5% on savings; the bank pays 0.1%. On a $2,000 savings balance for one year (simple interest), how much more would the credit union pay?

misconceptions.D: Uses only the credit union's interest

questions.set_title: Banks, credit unions, and what they do
questions.section_skill: Comparing financial institutions
questions.question: Which document lists every fee an account can charge, such as overdraft, wire, and paper statement fees?

choices.text: The bank's home page advertisement
The account's fee schedule
A monthly statement from last year
The debit card itself

questions.correct_answer: The account's fee schedule

misconceptions.C: Thinks a statement lists every possible fee
misconceptions.D: Thinks fees are printed on the card

questions.feedback: Banks give a fee schedule (often part of the account agreement). Ads show the highlights; the fee schedule shows every charge.

questions.set_title: Banks, credit unions, and what they do
questions.section_skill: Comparing financial institutions
questions.question: Leo picks a bank only because it gave him a $200 bonus for opening an account. Six months later he notices $15 monthly fees. What step did he skip?

choices.text: Asking the bank for a larger bonus before opening
Opening the account online
Reading the fee conditions before choosing
Getting a credit card from the same bank first

questions.correct_answer: Reading the fee conditions before choosing

misconceptions.A: Treats the bonus as the main decision
misconceptions.B: Thinks the method of opening caused the fees
misconceptions.D: Thinks a credit card prevents account fees

questions.feedback: Six months of $15 fees is $90, and the fees continue every month. Bonuses often require conditions; the fee rules decide the long-run cost.

questions.section_skill: Use a checking account and debit card and track the available balance
questions.intro: A checking account is a bank or credit union account for everyday money: receiving pay, paying bills, buying things with a debit card, and writing checks. Checking accounts usually pay little or no interest. Money you are setting aside for later usually goes in a savings account.
questions.question: Tia's paycheck is deposited into her checking account. Which use is a checking account designed for?

choices.text: Earning high interest on long-term savings
Paying rent, bills, and everyday purchases
Buying shares of stock
Borrowing money for a car

questions.correct_answer: Paying rent, bills, and everyday purchases

misconceptions.C: Confuses checking with a brokerage account
misconceptions.D: Confuses an account with a loan

questions.feedback: Checking accounts are transaction accounts for everyday spending and bills. Long-term savings and investments belong in other accounts.

questions.section_skill: Use a checking account and debit card and track the available balance
questions.intro: A debit card is linked to your checking account. When you pay with it, the money comes out of your account, usually within a day or two. A credit card is different: the card company lends you the money, and you pay it back later.
questions.question: Noah buys groceries for $46.30 with his debit card. Where does the money come from?

choices.text: Directly from Noah's checking account
From a loan that Noah repays next month
From the store's bank account
From Noah's savings account automatically, every time

questions.correct_answer: Directly from Noah's checking account

misconceptions.B: Confuses a debit card with a credit card
misconceptions.D: Thinks debit cards draw from savings

questions.feedback: A debit card spends money already in the linked checking account. It is not a loan.

questions.section_skill: Use a checking account and debit card and track the available balance
questions.intro: Your balance is the money in your account. Each withdrawal, debit card purchase, or bill payment is subtracted; each deposit is added. Keeping a running balance helps you avoid spending money you do not have.
questions.question: Ella's checking balance is $312.40. She pays a $95.25 phone bill and makes a $40.00 ATM withdrawal. What is her new balance?

misconceptions.D: Adds the payments instead of subtracting

questions.section_skill: Use a checking account and debit card and track the available balance
questions.intro: Some merchants, such as gas stations, hotels, and car rentals, place a temporary "hold" on a debit card before they know the final amount. The hold lowers your AVAILABLE balance (what you can spend now) until the final charge posts and the extra is released, often within a few days.
questions.question: At a gas pump, Sam's debit card is approved, and the bank places a $100 hold, even though Sam pumps only $38 of gas. What is the effect until the hold is released?

choices.text: Sam is charged $100 permanently
Sam's account balance goes up by $62
Nothing changes, because holds only apply to credit cards
Sam's available balance is $100 lower for a short time

questions.correct_answer: Sam's available balance is $100 lower for a short time

misconceptions.A: Thinks a hold is the final charge
misconceptions.C: Thinks holds only apply to credit cards

questions.feedback: The hold temporarily reduces the available balance by $100. When the $38 charge posts, the extra $62 is released.

questions.section_skill: Use a checking account and debit card and track the available balance
questions.intro: Federal law limits what you owe when a card is used without permission. For credit cards, the most you can owe for unauthorized charges is $50. For debit cards, the limit depends on how quickly you report the loss: $50, $500, or more if you wait over 60 days after your statement. Debit card fraud also removes your own money until the bank investigates.
questions.question: A thief steals Ava's wallet and uses both her debit card and her credit card. Which card generally gives her stronger legal protection against the thief's charges?

choices.text: The debit card, because it spends her own money
The debit card, because banks must refund theft the same day
The credit card
Both cards always have identical protection

questions.correct_answer: The credit card

misconceptions.A: Assumes spending your own money gives more protection

questions.feedback: Federal law caps credit card liability for unauthorized charges at $50. Debit card liability depends on how quickly you report the loss: up to $50, up to $500, or more after 60 days. Meanwhile, a thief has spent your own money.

questions.section_skill: Debit versus credit
questions.intro: "Debit" means taking money out of your account. A debit card takes money from your checking account. "Credit" means borrowing: a credit card company pays the store, and you owe the card company.
questions.question: Which card spends money that is ALREADY in your bank account?

choices.text: A debit card
A credit card
A store gift card from a friend
A library card

questions.correct_answer: A debit card

misconceptions.B: Thinks a credit card spends your own money
misconceptions.C: Confuses a prepaid gift card with a bank account card

questions.feedback: A debit card draws on money already in your checking account.

questions.section_skill: Debit versus credit
questions.intro: With a credit card, the card company pays the merchant for you. The amount is added to your card balance, which is a debt you must pay back. If you do not pay the full balance by the due date, you may owe interest.
questions.question: Owen pays for a $25 meal with a credit card. Who pays the restaurant first?

choices.text: Owen's checking account, immediately
The credit card company, and Owen owes it $25
The restaurant pays itself
Nobody pays the restaurant until Owen gets his monthly bill

questions.correct_answer: The credit card company, and Owen owes it $25

misconceptions.D: Thinks the store waits to be paid

questions.feedback: The card company pays the restaurant; Owen now owes the card company $25.

questions.section_skill: Debit versus credit
questions.intro: A debit card can only spend the money in your account. If a purchase is larger than your balance, the bank may decline it. If you opted in to overdraft coverage, the bank may pay it and charge an overdraft fee.
questions.question: What happens if you try to spend more with a debit card than your account holds?

choices.text: The extra amount becomes a free gift
The store lowers the price to your balance
Your credit card is charged automatically, every time
It is declined, or covered for an overdraft fee

questions.correct_answer: It is declined, or covered for an overdraft fee

misconceptions.A: Thinks the bank absorbs the shortfall for free
misconceptions.B: Thinks the store adjusts the price
misconceptions.C: Thinks a credit card always backs a debit card

questions.feedback: Spending past your balance leads to a declined purchase or an overdraft with a fee.

questions.section_skill: Debit versus credit
questions.question: Which statement is TRUE?

choices.text: Using a debit card creates a debt; using a credit card does not
Both cards always create a debt
Using a credit card creates a debt; using a debit card does not
Neither card is ever connected to money you owe

questions.correct_answer: Using a credit card creates a debt; using a debit card does not
questions.feedback: Credit cards are borrowing. Debit cards spend your own money.

questions.section_skill: Debit versus credit
questions.intro: If you do not opt in to overdraft coverage, a bank generally cannot charge you an overdraft fee for an ATM withdrawal or a one-time debit card purchase; instead the purchase is declined. A credit card lets you borrow up to a credit limit, which is not your money.
questions.question: Mia wants a card that will stop her from spending more than she has. Which card fits that goal better?

choices.text: A credit card with a high limit
A debit card with overdraft coverage turned off
A credit card that she uses only for large purchases
Any card, because cards cannot be overspent

questions.correct_answer: A debit card with overdraft coverage turned off

misconceptions.A: Thinks a credit limit is her own money
misconceptions.C: Thinks purchase size changes how credit works

questions.feedback: Without overdraft coverage, one-time debit card purchases above the balance are generally declined, so Mia cannot spend money she does not have.

questions.section_skill: ATM networks and fees
questions.intro: An ATM network is a group of machines your bank lets you use without a fee. At an "out-of-network" ATM you can be charged twice: once by your own bank and once by the ATM's owner (a "surcharge").
questions.question: Rosa uses an out-of-network ATM. Her bank charges $2.50 and the ATM owner charges $3.00. She withdraws $40. How much leaves her account in total?

misconceptions.C: Includes only the ATM owner's fee

questions.section_skill: ATM networks and fees
questions.intro: Small fees repeated often add up. Multiply the fee per use by the number of uses in a year.
questions.question: Rosa makes that same kind of out-of-network withdrawal twice a week. About how much does she pay in ATM fees in a year (52 weeks)?

misconceptions.A: Gives the fees for one withdrawal
misconceptions.D: Includes the $40 cash withdrawn each time

questions.feedback: Fees per withdrawal: $2.50 + $3.00 = $5.50. Withdrawals per year: 2 × 52 = 104. Fees: $5.50 × 104 = $572.

questions.section_skill: ATM networks and fees
questions.question: Which choice would cut Rosa's ATM fees the MOST?

choices.text: Use in-network ATMs or get cash back at stores
Withdraw $20 each time instead of $40
Use a different out-of-network ATM each time she needs cash
Check her balance at the ATM before each withdrawal

questions.correct_answer: Use in-network ATMs or get cash back at stores

misconceptions.B: Smaller withdrawals mean more fees, not fewer
misconceptions.C: Thinks a different machine avoids fees

questions.feedback: In-network ATMs and cash back at stores usually have no fees. Smaller, more frequent withdrawals raise the total fees.

questions.section_skill: ATM networks and fees
questions.intro: Some accounts refund ATM fees up to a monthly limit. The refund lowers what you pay, but only up to that limit.
questions.question: A bank refunds up to $10 of other banks' ATM fees each month. Rosa pays $22 in out-of-network fees this month. How much does she pay after the refund?

misconceptions.A: Gives the refund instead of what she pays

questions.section_skill: ATM networks and fees
questions.question: Which statement about an ATM "balance inquiry" at an out-of-network machine is MOST accurate?

choices.text: It is always free, because no money leaves the account
It moves money to savings
It counts as a deposit
It can carry a fee even though no money is withdrawn

questions.correct_answer: It can carry a fee even though no money is withdrawn

misconceptions.A: Assumes balance checks are free at any ATM
misconceptions.B: Confuses an inquiry with a transfer
misconceptions.C: Confuses an inquiry with a deposit

questions.feedback: Out-of-network ATMs may charge for balance checks. Checking the balance in your bank's app is usually free.

questions.section_skill: Pending transactions, available balance, and posting
questions.intro: A transaction is "pending" when the bank knows about it but has not finished processing it ("posting" it). Your available balance is the money you can spend now: roughly your posted balance minus pending charges and holds. Spending based on the larger number can cause overdrafts.
questions.question: Kim's app shows: current balance $250; pending transactions −$80. What is her available balance?

questions.section_skill: Pending transactions, available balance, and posting
questions.intro: Bank apps show what the bank knows. A check you wrote that the payee has not cashed yet does not appear at all. Your own record of payments, called a register, catches those.
questions.question: Which balance should Kim use to decide whether she can afford a $150 purchase today?

choices.text: The highest balance she had this month
Her balance from last month's statement
Her available balance minus uncleared checks
Her current balance, without counting pending items

questions.correct_answer: Her available balance minus uncleared checks
questions.feedback: Her real spending power is the available balance minus payments the bank has not seen yet.

questions.section_skill: Pending transactions, available balance, and posting
questions.intro: When you deposit a check, the bank may "hold" part of the money until the check clears. Federal rules set the maximum hold times, and the bank must tell you when the money will be available.
questions.question: Ben deposits a $600 check on Monday. The bank says $225 is available Tuesday and the rest Thursday. How much can Ben safely spend from this deposit on Tuesday?

misconceptions.D: Assumes the whole deposit is available at once
misconceptions.C: Gives the amount held until Thursday
misconceptions.A: Thinks none of a check is available early

questions.feedback: Only $225 is available Tuesday; the remaining $375 becomes available Thursday.

questions.section_skill: Pending transactions, available balance, and posting
questions.question: If a deposited check "bounces" (is returned unpaid) after you spent the money, what usually happens?

choices.text: The bank takes the amount back from your account, possibly with a fee
The bank keeps the money in your account because it was already available
The person who wrote the check pays your fee
Nothing, because the deposit was already posted

questions.correct_answer: The bank takes the amount back from your account, possibly with a fee

misconceptions.C: Assumes fees are always passed on

questions.section_skill: Compare checking accounts and complete the steps to open one
questions.intro: Banks and credit unions usually require an adult (18 or older) to open an account alone, because a minor generally cannot be held to a contract. Wait until age 21, the legal minimum age for any bank account

misconceptions.B: Invents a minimum age for every account

questions.section_skill: Compare checking accounts and complete the steps to open one
questions.intro: Federal rules require banks to verify who opens an account. Name, birth date, address, and an ID number such as an SSN

Account X: $120; Account Y: $0

The bank takes $12 each month unless a waiver applies
You must deposit $12 every month to keep the account open

questions.intro: A waiver condition is a rule that, if you meet it, cancels a fee. A "minimum daily balance" rule means your balance must stay at or above the amount every day of the statement period.

questions.question: Which statement about a minimum opening deposit is TRUE?

questions.section_skill: Reading account disclosures and fee schedules
questions.intro: When you open an account, the bank gives you disclosures: documents that list the account's interest rate, fees, and rules. Federal law (the Truth in Savings Act) requires banks to disclose this information. Small optional fees, like paper statement fees, are easy to miss.
questions.question: A disclosure says: "Paper statement fee: $2 per month. Free with e-statements." Rafael wants paper statements. Over two years, how much will this choice cost?
questions.feedback: $2 per month × 24 months = $48.

questions.section_skill: Reading account disclosures and fee schedules
questions.intro: A fee schedule is a list of every fee the account can charge: monthly fees, overdraft and returned item fees, wire transfer fees, stop payment fees, out-of-network ATM fees, and fees for extras like paper statements or cashier's checks.
questions.question: Which item would you expect to find in an account's fee schedule?

choices.text: The bank's current interest rate on 30-year home mortgages
The FDIC insurance limit for your account
The charge for an incoming or outgoing wire transfer
The interest rate on your credit card

misconceptions.A: Confuses a fee schedule with a loan rate sheet
misconceptions.D: Confuses a deposit fee schedule with a card agreement

questions.feedback: Wire transfer fees are account fees listed in a fee schedule.

questions.section_skill: Reading account disclosures and fee schedules
questions.question: An account advertises "No monthly fee!" Its fee schedule lists a $35 overdraft fee, a $3 out-of-network ATM fee, and a $30 wire fee. Which conclusion is correct?

choices.text: The account can still be costly, depending on how it is used
The account has no fees of any kind
The account will cost exactly $68 every month, since all three fees apply
Every one of those fees is illegal for a free account

questions.section_skill: Reading account disclosures and fee schedules
questions.intro: Banks can change account terms. They must tell existing customers in advance about changes that could hurt them, such as a higher fee. That notice gives you time to compare and decide.
questions.question: A bank sends a notice that a fee will change in 30 days. What is a reasonable response?

choices.text: Ignore it, because fees cannot change after an account is opened
Close the account the same day without checking alternatives
Pay the new fee now to lock in the old rate
Compare the new terms with other accounts

questions.correct_answer: Compare the new terms with other accounts

misconceptions.A: Thinks account terms are fixed forever
misconceptions.C: Invents a way to lock in fees

questions.feedback: Advance notice lets you compare and, if needed, move your money before the change takes effect.

questions.section_skill: Reading account disclosures and fee schedules
questions.question: Which question is MOST useful when comparing two accounts' disclosures?

Which fees will I realistically pay, given how I bank?
Which disclosure document is longer?
Which bank's advertising do I see most often on social media?

misconceptions.C: Uses document length as a measure of cost
misconceptions.D: Uses advertising as a measure of cost

questions.section_skill: Account screening and second-chance accounts
questions.intro: Before opening an account, many banks check a consumer report from a checking account screening company, such as ChexSystems or Early Warning Services. choices.text: Grades and attendance from high school
Devon's medical history and doctor visits
Every purchase Devon has made with cash
Unpaid overdrafts or fraud at past banks

questions.correct_answer: Unpaid overdrafts or fraud at past banks
questions.feedback: Screening reports focus on past deposit-account problems, such as unpaid negative balances or fraud.

questions.section_skill: Account screening and second-chance accounts
questions.intro: Checking account screening companies are consumer reporting agencies. Under federal law you can get a free copy of your report every 12 months and dispute information you believe is wrong; the company must investigate.
questions.question: Devon thinks the report has a mistake. What can he do?

choices.text: Nothing, because screening reports cannot be corrected
Pay the screening company to delete it
Request a free copy of the report and dispute the error
Open new accounts under a friend's name instead of his own

questions.correct_answer: Request a free copy of the report and dispute the error
questions.feedback: Like credit reports, screening reports can be requested for free each year and disputed when wrong.

questions.section_skill: Account screening and second-chance accounts
questions.question: Devon's report is accurate: he left a $90 negative balance at an old bank. Which step would most likely help him open an account in the future?

Wait one week, because reports clear automatically
Open many applications at once to find one bank that says yes
Avoid banks and keep all of his money in cash

questions.section_skill: Account screening and second-chance accounts
questions.intro: Some banks and credit unions offer second-chance accounts to people who were denied regular accounts. They may have a monthly fee, no overdraft feature, or lower limits. After a period of good use, some can be changed to a regular account.

A loan that pays off your old bank's balance
A savings account that pays double interest
An account for people with past account problems, often with limits

questions.intro: Reconciling means checking that your records match the bank's. questions.correct_answer: A stop payment order through her bank
questions.feedback: A stop payment order tells the bank not to pay that check, if it has not already cleared.

questions.section_skill: Payment app safety
questions.intro: A common scam claims you received money "by mistake" and asks you to send it back. Sometimes the original payment was made with stolen information and is later reversed, leaving you with the loss. Verify inside your own app or bank, never through a link or message.
questions.question: Someone texts Ava: "I sent you $200 by mistake — please send it back!" Her app shows no new money in her account. What should she do?

choices.text: Send $200 back right away to be polite
Check her own account directly and send nothing
Reply with her bank login so they can fix it
Send $100 as a compromise

questions.correct_answer: Check her own account directly and send nothing

misconceptions.D: Still sends money to a scammer

questions.feedback: Without verified money in her own account, there is nothing to return. Even if money did arrive, contact the app's support rather than sending money.

questions.section_skill: Payment app safety
questions.question: Which setting adds the most protection to a payment app?

choices.text: Sharing your login with a parent and a friend so they can watch for fraud
Using the same password as your email
Turning off notifications
Multi-factor authentication and a passcode on the app

questions.correct_answer: Multi-factor authentication and a passcode on the app
questions.feedback: Multi-factor authentication and an app passcode make unauthorized access much harder.

questions.section_skill: Payment app safety
questions.intro: Real banks and payment apps do not ask you to move money to a "safe account" to protect it. Imposters pretend to be bank staff, tech support, or government officials and create urgency.
questions.question: A "customer support" caller says your payment app is hacked and asks you to send your balance to a "safe account." What is this?

choices.text: A standard security procedure
A government requirement
An imposter scam
A way to earn extra interest

questions.correct_answer: An imposter scam

misconceptions.A: Real companies do not ask this

questions.feedback: Any request to move money to protect it is a red flag for an imposter scam. Hang up and call the official number.

questions.section_skill: Payment app safety
questions.question: Which payment is generally protected under federal error rules (Regulation E)?

choices.text: A transfer someone else made from your account without permission
A payment you chose to send to an online seller who never shipped
A payment you sent to the wrong person after typing their name
Money you lost gambling with an app

questions.correct_answer: A transfer someone else made from your account without permission
questions.feedback: Regulation E protections focus on unauthorized transfers and certain errors; payments you authorize, even to scammers, are often not covered.

questions.section_skill: Payment app safety
questions.question: Before sending money with a payment app to someone new, which step lowers the risk the MOST?

choices.text: Sending a small test payment to a stranger
Confirming who the recipient is through a source you trust
Checking that the stranger's profile has a photo and many friends
Asking the stranger to promise to deliver

questions.correct_answer: Confirming who the recipient is through a source you trust
questions.feedback: Verifying who you are paying, through a channel you trust, prevents most P2P losses.
